content:
Hi everyone,

I created a library called Litlib to solve a problem I ran into while formalizing properties of a Spin(4, C) gauge field. The issue is that a lot of the mathematical machinery I needed to access was published and peer-reviewed, but it's completely infeasible to formalize all of that historical literature from scratch just so I could use it in my own research. My solution ended up working fantastically well.

The core idea is that a paper's equation or theorem can be transcribed into a class. Then, downstream, I can inject this class as an instance variable into my own derivations.

Here is a minimally working example of the pattern:

-- Transcribe a specific equation/theorem from a paper as an axiomatic class
class Litlib.evans2026example.Eq42 (A : Type) [Add A] where
     paper_identity : ∀ (a b : A), a + b = b + a

-- Use the unformalized literature as a strict dependency in your new theorem
theorem my_novel_research {A : Type} [Add A] [eq42 : Litlib.evans2026example.Eq42 A] (x y : A) :
     (x + y) + x = x + (y + x) := by
     rw [eq42.paper_identity x y]

Reading the code, it's immediately obvious where the unformalized boundary is.

To support this, I also built CLI tools that will print out the code summary for any theorem(s) (extracting specified signatures without the proof, as well as all relevant non-Mathlib definitions). I also wrote a formatter that outputs this code summary so it can work directly as an appendix in a LaTeX paper, including hyperlinks to definitions/theorems, with the Litlib dependencies cited in the bibliography.

I built this tool for my own purposes, and it works well enough that I'll keep maintaining it. However, it's useful enough that I suspect it could be valuable for others doing applied math or physics in Lean.

If you want to give it a try, send me a note! At this phase, it's easy enough to hammer out new features or change idiosyncrasies that I found useful but that might not fit your specific workflow.

It might be interesting to see if there's any way to use this to begin 'outlining' what still needs to be formalized (and/or to see what recent papers can be more easily connected to what has already been formalized)

A. Young said:

It might be interesting to see if there's any way to use this to begin 'outlining' what still needs to be formalized (and/or to see what recent papers can be more easily connected to what has already been formalized)

This feature exists in a basic form already!

(nix:nix-shell-env) logan@P1ckax:~/Repos/chiral-gauge-dynamics$ cgd-report --dashboard=kinematicActionQuantization

====================================================================
                        CGD DASHBOARD
====================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------
[STANDALONE THEOREMS]

 ✔ Topological Action Quantization (CGD.Quantum.kinematicActionQuantization)
    ├─ Depends on: belavin1975pseudoparticle Eq 8 (⚠ Unformalized)
    └─ Depends on: nakahara2003geometry Eq 10.128 (⚠ Unformalized)

Total Standalone Theorems: 1  |  Fully Proved: 1  |  Incomplete: 0

This checks the Litlib classes for a proof body, and in those two examples, that's missing, so Eq 8 and Eq 10.128 are straight up transcriptions of textbook/paper results. The example kinematicActionQuantization has a proof body that contains no sorrys, so it gets a green checkmark.

I can imagine various ways to enhance this functionality; instead of just looking for a sorry, it could also look for opaque, usage of an axiom in the proof body, class inputs that are not in Litlib... for me, the most useful feature would be to count how many hypotheses a theorem has so that I could quickly identify which theorems to inspect with a full --code-summary.

As for "outlining" with Litlib, you would create a bunch of theorems and toss a sorry into the proof body. Constructing a graphviz dependency chart (similar to what Lean Blueprint does, but tracking the Litlib dependencies) could happen, but doesn't currently exist. Adding the ability to annotate todos in a theorem could be useful (e.g. add litlib_todo("This theorem should depend on ABC")).

What kinds of outlining features would need to exist for your workflow?
